NEW YORK (CNN) -- New York's iconic Plaza Hotel will lose a figure nearly as synonymous with it as Eloise when its longest-serving doorman retires Thursday after 46 years on the job. Ed Trinka, whose retirement coincides with his 65th birthday, joined the hotel 1963. Ed Trinka, whose retirement coincides with his 65th birthday, joined the hotel's staff in 1963 as a teenager. He spent 40 years at the fabled lodging's Fifth Avenue entrance, relocating to its doorway facing Central Park South during the property's renovation and partial conversion to condominiums several years ago. Now as much a Central Park South fixture as the horse-drawn carriages that line the park's southern perimeter, the gregarious Trinka is known as the "mayor of 59th Street." On a recent afternoon, he seemed to know every other passerby, exchanging a constant stream of hellos with chauffeurs and doormen from adjacent tony apartment buildings and, of course, the Plaza's residents. Over his more than four decades manning the Plaza's entrance, Trinka has met countless celebrities -- or "all of them," as he puts it. After his first celebrity encounter at the hotel with the Beatles, he's catered to a long procession of big names, including Joe DiMaggio, Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and Liza Minnelli. Marla Maples, ex-wife of one-time Plaza owner Donald Trump, would regularly peck Trinka on the cheek when she saw him. Trinka says he has an autographed photo of Richard Nixon -- a token of gratitude from the former president -- hanging on proud display at his home. Trinka says he has thoroughly enjoyed his lengthy stay at the portal to history and glamour. "I never had a bad day in all the years." Nonetheless, with all those years at the hotel under his belt, Trinka felt it was time to "bow out gracefully." As he transitions to retirement, Trinka says he'll miss the front-row view of Central Park and the hotel's clientele -- the "greatest people in the world." He also concedes he'll miss "the women." The building's inhabitants are not eager for his departure. "He's a gentleman, refined -- you don't find these people anymore," lamented resident Joan Spain. Trinka's replacement, Jimmy O'Connell, is keenly aware of the large shoes he'll have to fill, saying he'd be satisfied if he "could be half the doorman" Trinka is. The hotel will bid farewell to Trinka in characteristically grand fashion on Thursday afternoon. After a champagne send-off in the hotel's landmarked Oak Room, its management will present him with an opportunity to view the Plaza from the vantage point of the countless guests he's greeted over the years: He'll be given a free stay at the hotel. In addition to a trove of anecdotes about celebrities, Trinka acquired something else during his tenure at the Plaza: a new name. Years ago, the hotel gave him a nametag that mistakenly read Edward, even though his full name is Edwin. He came to embrace the errant nametag, neglecting to correct people when they called him Edward and even naming his own son Edward.

**End of an era: The Plaza’s longest-serving doorman hangs up his top hat after 46 years**

By **CNN Staff**

**NEW YORK (CNN) —** For nearly half a century, he was the first face visitors saw at New York City’s most famous address. Now, Ed Trinka, the legendary lead doorman at The Plaza Hotel, is taking his final bow. 

After 46 years of opening car doors, hailing cabs, and greeting guests at Fifth Avenue and Central Park South, Trinka officially retired this week, marking the end of an unprecedented career in American hospitality. 

Trinka began his journey at The Plaza in the late 1970s as a young man looking for a steady gig. Over the next four and a half decades, he outlasted multiple hotel ownerships—including the eras of Donald Trump and Saudi Prince Al-Waleed bin Talal—and witnessed the city’s dramatic evolution, all from the hotel’s iconic brass-and-red-carpet entrance. 

"When you put on that coat, you’re not just representing a hotel, you’re representing New York City," Trinka, 68, told CNN in an interview on his final day. "I’ve seen it all—the good times, the tough times, and everything in between. But the secret to this job has always been simple: treat the king like a regular guy, and treat the regular guy like a king."

During his tenure, Trinka’s white-gloved hands opened doors for world leaders, foreign royalty, and Hollywood icons. From Elizabeth Taylor and Michael Jackson to U.S. presidents and international heads of state, Trinka was a constant, steady presence. He was also a fixture on set during the countless film shoots hosted at the historic landmark, including the 1992 classic *Home Alone 2: Lost in New York*.

To hotel guests, he was a master of discretion and charm. To his colleagues, he was the undisputed "Mayor of 59th Street."

Hotel management and staff gathered in The Plaza's Grand Ballroom on Thursday afternoon for a emotional farewell ceremony, presenting Trinka with a framed brass door handle and a customized golden whistle. 

"Ed isn't just an employee; he is part of the architectural fabric of The Plaza," said Luigi Romaniello, Managing Director of The Plaza. "His warmth, his sharp eye, and his unwavering standard of service set the tone for the entire luxury hotel industry. Replacing him is quite literally impossible."

Standing at the Grand Army Plaza entrance through blistering summer heatwaves, freezing winter blizzards, and the quiet streets of the city during the pandemic, Trinka estimates he has opened well over two million doors in his career. 

Despite the physical demands of standing for hours on hard pavement and the shift toward modern, digital hotel check-ins, Trinka maintained that the human element of his role could never be replaced by technology. 

"A smartphone can't smile at you when you look lost, and an app can't hand you an umbrella just before the sky breaks open," Trinka said. "People come to New York looking for magic, and the doorman is the person who hands them the key to it."

As for his retirement plans, Trinka says he looks forward to spending time with his family, traveling, and—for the first time in nearly five decades—letting someone else open the door for him. 

"It’s been an incredible ride," Trinka said, tipping his signature top hat one last time before stepping into the afternoon sun. "I came here looking for a job, and I’m leaving with a lifetime of memories."

**The Last Watch on Fifth Avenue: NYC’s Most Belated Keeper of Secrets Bids Farewell**

**NEW YORK —** For 42 years, the brass handles of 1040 Fifth Avenue didn’t just open doors—they held the secrets, sorrows, and quiet triumphs of Manhattan’s elite. And the man holding them was always Arthur “Artie” Vance.

Standing 6-foot-2 in his immaculate, gold-trimmed navy overcoat, white gloves crisp despite the damp November drizzle, 68-year-old Artie has been a fixture of the Upper East Side since 1981. He has survived eight mayoral administrations, three major recessions, a pandemic, and the transition from rotary phones to smart home apps. 

On Thursday night, the legendary doorman worked his final shift.

“People think this job is about muscle and umbrella management,” Artie said, his eyes crinkling at the corners as he polished the building’s brass plaque one last time. “It’s not. It’s about rhythm. You gotta read the sidewalk. You gotta know who needs a joke, who needs silence, and who needs you to pretend you didn't see who they came home with.”

### **Coffee with Bowie and Quiet Nights with Jackie**

In four decades on Fifth Avenue, Artie has had a front-row seat to American pop culture. But true to the strict code of the Union of Building Service Employees (32BJ), discretion was always his highest currency. Now that he is officially off the clock, he allows himself a few fond recollections.

There was the blizzard of 1988, when David Bowie, staying with a resident in the building, found himself stranded in the lobby waiting for a black car that was never coming. 

“He sat right there on the velvet bench,” Artie recalled, gesturing to a polished mahogany entryway. “We shared black coffee out of my thermos and talked about the Brooklyn Dodgers for two hours. He was just a guy in a big coat who was cold. Didn't ask for a picture, didn't ask for an autograph. He gave me a crisp hundred-dollar bill and a nod every Christmas after that.”

Then there were the quiet moments with Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, who lived down the block and often strolled past on her evening walks. 

“She had a way of walking—very light, like she didn't want to wake up the city,” Artie said. “One evening, her scarf blew off in a gust off Central Park. I caught it before it hit the puddle. She smiled, touched my arm, and said, ‘Thank you, Arthur. You’re my hero today.’ I didn't wash those gloves for a month.”

Artie also recalled dodging paparazzi with a young Leonardo DiCaprio in the late 1990s, guiding the actor through the building’s service entrance in a laundry cart. "He was terrified," Artie chuckled. "I told him, 'Kid, just keep your head down and let the door shut. Nobody gets past the glass.'"

### **The Heartbeat of 1040**

While the celebrity encounters make for good party stories, it is the ordinary, everyday intimacy of the job that Artie says he will miss most. Over 42 years, he has raised three generations of residents. He has remembered thousands of dog names, held keys for cheating spouses and secret lovers, and comforted widows on their first night alone in cavernous 12-room apartments.

“Artie is the nervous system of this building,” said Eleanor Roth, 84, a resident who has lived on the eighth floor since 1975. “When my husband had his heart attack in 1996, Artie was up in our apartment before the paramedics. He held my hand in the elevator. You can buy real estate in New York, but you cannot buy an Artie.”

For younger residents, Artie was a grandfather figure wrapped in a wool uniform. 

“I used to come home from school in fifth grade, forget my key, and sit at the desk with Artie eating half his sandwich,” said Julian Vance-Harris, 29, an attorney who grew up in the building. “He knew when I got my first heartbreak, he knew when I passed the bar, and he was the first person I showed my baby to when we brought her home from the hospital. Walking through those doors without him is going to feel like entering a different building.”

### **A Champagne Send-Off**

On Thursday at 5:00 PM, the usually serene, museum-quiet lobby of 1040 Fifth Avenue exploded into applause. 

Nearly 100 current and former residents—alongside fellow doormen from neighboring buildings along the Park—packed the marble foyer. Crystal champagne flutes rested on the mail desk. Children who Artie once walked to the school bus, now adults in tailored suits, lined up to hug him.

The Co-op Board presented Artie with a custom-engraved brass door handle mounted on mahogany, along with an envelope detailing a resident-funded retirement gift: an all-expenses-paid, six-month trip to Italy for Artie and his wife, Rosa, followed by a quiet villa stay in his ancestral hometown in Sicily.

When it came time for Artie to speak, the man who had commanded Fifth Avenue traffic with a single blown whistle choked back tears.

“A building is just limestone and steel,” Artie told the crowded lobby, hanging his white gloves on the bell captain's desk. “It’s the people who give it a soul. Thank you for letting me guard yours for forty-two years.”

At precisely 7:00 PM, Artie unbuttoned his heavy coat, handed the brass key to his successor—a 28-year-old named Marcus whom Artie has mentored for six months—and stepped out onto Fifth Avenue. 

This time, someone else held the door for him.
